listenings.text: Renato, great heat this morning. Second place, you advanced! Your quarterfinal is at two, so here's the plan for the next three hours. First, eat something now, so that you have energy at two and your stomach isn't full in the water. A sandwich and some fruit, not a big pie. Then go and sit in the shade under the club tent, to get out of the sun and stay hydrated. Drink a full bottle of water before one o'clock. At one fifteen, come and find me. We're going to watch heat one together, in order to see where the sets are breaking in the afternoon. The tide is going to be higher, so the peak moves a little. And at one thirty, jog and stretch to warm up your muscles. After that, no phone. Just breathe and focus. Okay? Go eat.

So you want to know my routine? Okay. On heat day I wake up really early, to check the waves before everybody else. I always eat the same breakfast, eggs on toast, so that my stomach feels normal. I write my heat time on my hand with a pen, so that I don't forget it. Yeah, I forgot it once, and I nearly missed my heat. Then, an hour before, I give my phone to Jess, so that I can't look at it. The phone is my biggest distraction. And in the last five minutes I sit on my board in the shallow water, to feel the ocean before the horn. That's it. Today it didn't work, but it usually does. Steal it if you want.

paras: Leah Kemp is twenty-two, and she surfs on the pro tour. She grew up in a small beach town in Western Australia, and she started surfing at eight. Before every heat, she follows the same routine. "I do the same things every time so that my body knows what's coming," she says. "A good routine helps me to stay calm."

Her routine starts sixty minutes before the horn. First she eats a banana and some nuts to get energy. She drinks a lot of water in order to stay hydrated, because the sun on the beach is strong. Then she watches the ocean for ten minutes to see where the sets are breaking.

Thirty minutes before her heat, Leah jogs on the sand to warm up her muscles, and she stretches so that she doesn't get hurt. After that, she sits down, closes her eyes and breathes slowly. She imagines her best waves in order to prepare her mind.

In the last ten minutes, she puts on her headphones so that she can't hear the crowd. "The crowd is a big distraction," she explains. "I listen to the same three songs to keep my focus." And her advice for young surfers? "Don't copy my routine. Find your own, and use it every time."
